text:
COURT OF
APPEAL FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Wise v. Broadway Properties Ltd.,

2005 BCCA 546

Date: 20051107

Docket: CA032723

Between:

Norman D. Wise

Appellant

(
Plaintiff
)

And

Broadway Properties Ltd.

Respondent

(
Defendant
)

Before:

The Honourable Madam Justice Prowse

The Honourable Mr. Justice Donald

The Honourable Madam Justice Kirkpatrick

N.R. Howell

Counsel
for the Appellant

S.R. Stark

Counsel
for the Respondent

Place and Date
of Hearing:

Vancouver, British Columbia

17 October 2005

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
British Columbia

7
November 2005

Written Reasons by
:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Donald

Concurred in by:

The Honourable Madam Justice Prowse

The Honourable Madam Justice Kirkpatrick

Reasons for
Judgment of the Honourable Mr. Justice Donald:

[
1
]

After working for approximately 10 years as
resident caretaker of an apartment block in West Vancouver owned by Broadway
Properties Ltd. ("Broadway"), Norman D. Wise ("Wise")
threatened to sue Broadway for the value of unpaid work and directed a
particularly offensive insult at the principal of Broadway.

[
2
]

Broadway fired him.

[
3
]

Wise brought an action for unjust enrichment
claiming $179,676.54 and damages for wrongful dismissal.  Broadway counterclaimed
to recover over-payment of vacation pay.

[
4
]

On 4 February 2005, Mr. Justice Johnston
dismissed Wise's claim and Broadway's counterclaim:  (4 February 2005),
Vancouver S012489 (B.C.S.C.).

[
5
]

Wise brings this appeal from the dismissal of
his claims.  His factum alleges the following errors in the judgment below:

1.         The trial judge erred in law in
finding that the claim for
quantum meruit
was not made out.

2.         The trial judge's finding of
cause cannot reasonably be supported on the evidence for the following reasons:

a)         The
trial judge erred in finding that while neither a threat to sue nor the
reference to Jewish labour, standing alone, amounted to cause, when combined
together they did amount to cause;

b)         The trial judge erred
by failing to consider a full contextual analysis of the misconduct as set out
by the Supreme Court of Canada in
McKinley v. BC Tel

2001 SCC 38 (CanLII)
, [2001]
S.C.J. No. 40 (SCC).

[
6
]

The
quantum meruit
claim relates to a
range of duties ordinarily performed by property managers, as distinct from caretakers.
In Wise's view, those duties went well beyond what he was paid for as a
resident caretaker.  His grievance, which he harboured for several years prior
to termination, seems to focus on his setting rents for the units and hiring and
supervising contractors for maintenance and improvements in the building.  He
began performing those tasks when Broadway discontinued its engagement of an
outside property management firm.  That firm charged a fee of 3.5 per cent of
the gross rentals.  Wise used that formula as the basis for valuing his extra
services.

[
7
]

In challenging the dismissal of the
quantum
meruit
claim, Wise alleges an error of law.  But the argument on his behalf
is really about the trial judge's application of the law to the facts.  Since
Wise does not say that the trial judge got the law wrong or applied incorrect
principles, his appeal is one of mixed fact and law and accordingly the
standard of review requires more deference to the trial judge's findings.

[
8
]

Wise said that he pressed the principal of
Broadway, Al Roadburg ("Roadburg"), on a number of occasions to
compensate him for extra duties.  But, according to Wise, Roadburg either
ignored him or put him off with vague responses.  Yet Wise carried on; he
received raises in his caretaker's salary and he accepted extra payments for
work performed in improving the units.  In light of this evidence, the trial
judge was not satisfied Wise made out a case of unjust enrichment.  He said in his
reasons for judgment:

[41]      There is also some evidence that when
Mr. Wise did some things that were considered by both parties to be above and
beyond his property management duties, he billed for and was paid for it at a
$15 per hour rate.  That, I take as an indication that while the precise
outlines of the job description under which Mr. Wise was working may not have
been crystal clear, the parties, at least during the currency of the job had a
pretty good working knowledge of what was expected and what his duties were and
had apparently no real difficulties sorting out when Mr. Wise was putting in
time or effort above and beyond what his monthly salary required of him and he
was remunerated for that.

[42]      This aspect of the claim and this is
the property management claim that is one of the lynchpins of the threat of
litigation and also forms, I recognize, a separate claim advanced in these
proceedings although not argued on a
quantum meruit
claim, the indicia
of
quantum meruit
clearly calls on me to consider whether that remedy is
appropriate having found that there is no contractual basis for remuneration.
I consider whether it is resting on unjust enrichment or restitution, whether
quantum
meruit
has been established or the right to be compensated in
quantum
meruit
has been established.

[43]      As I say, it was not particularly
argued on that basis and I have reviewed the evidence available.  I understand
Mr. Wise to be saying that he has suffered deprivation by way of holidays he
did not get, personal time he did not get off, extra effort he put in.  He
argues that the defendant has been substantially enriched as a result through
improvements to the building, increased rental revenue and property management
fees that the defendant has not had to pay since 1994.

[44]      All of that is some evidence that
might be capable of supporting an inference that
quantum meruit
would be
appropriate but I find on reviewing it and I did go over it at some length,
that
the evidence was simply not sufficient to establish to the degree
necessary the necessary elements of benefit, deprivation and the lack of
juristic reason necessary to invoke the equitable remedy
.

[Emphasis added.]

[
9
]

Assuming that Wise suffered a deprivation and
Broadway enjoyed a corresponding benefit — the trial judge did not make a clear
finding in this regard —Wise has not established the third element of unjust
enrichment; namely, the absence of a juridical reason, in circumstances where
he maintained and renewed his contractual relations, notwithstanding
dissatisfaction with his pay.  If Wise felt he was underpaid he could have
walked away from the relationship.  In my view, he could not build up an
equitable claim simply by carrying on in those circumstances.

[
10
]

I would not interfere with the dismissal of the
quantum
meruit
claim.

[
11
]

Moving to the wrongful dismissal ground, I need
to elaborate further on the facts.

[
12
]

In a state of exasperation after attempting to
discuss with Roadburg his belief that he was owed compensation for performing
property management duties, Wise wrote a five-page letter addressed to Roadburg
venting his frustration at the perceived injustice of his unpaid work.  The
letter is dated 23 June 1999.  It contains the insult which forms one of the
grounds of his dismissal.  Wise decided not to send the letter, but he kept it.

[
13
]

Then in January 2001, Wise had a serious
disagreement with a tenant he suspected had stolen his towels from the laundry
room.  The tenant complained of Wise's behaviour to Broadway.  Wise felt that
Broadway unfairly took the tenant's side in the dispute.  This prompted him to
write another letter, this one dated 23 January 2001, also directed to
Roadburg.  Regrettably he enclosed the earlier letter.  Both letters make claim
compensation for the extra work.  In closing the second letter Wise wrote:

A Civil action
appears to be the only way in which I can get some closure out of being USED by
Broadway Properties in the case of the towels, AND in the case of not being
recompensed for acting as PROPERTY MANAGER since April of 1992 at 1875 Bellevue
Ave, in West Vancouver.  Let your conscience and fairness be your guide sir.

[
14
]

Broadway took this to be a threat to sue and a
repudiation of the employment relationship.  The trial judge said that by
itself it did not provide sufficient cause for dismissal.

[
15
]

The offending part of the first letter is as
follows:

You gave me a
building management and subsequently a
PROPERTY MANAGEMENT job, April of
1992, here at Village Towers.
.
I have undoubtedly fulfilled your
expectations in this regard, and I do not expect to be treated as the
unfortunate Jews were treated when impressed into working without pay for
Mercedes Benz, Volkswagen and Siemens during the Second World War.

[Emphasis added.]

[
16
]

Roadburg, a Jewish man then in his 80s (he died
before trial), was deeply offended by this comparison.

[
17
]

The trial judge found that the insult, along
with the threat to sue, constituted just cause.  He instructed himself on the
need to consider the offensive comparison in context:
McKinley v. BC Tel
,
[2001] 2 S.C.R. 161,
2001 SCC 38
.  His contextual analysis of the evidence
appears in the following excerpt from his reasons:

[47]      Going back to the contextual analysis
that the Supreme Court of Canada in
McKinley

would suggest I
should employ and which Mr. Justice Sigurdson said was appropriate in
Styba

[
v. University of British Columbia Employees Society, No. 116,

[1995] B.C.J. No. 2764 (QL)
], I say the context in which that passage is to be
read includes that to the knowledge of Mr. Wise, Mr. Roadburg, to whom it was
addressed, was Jewish, in his mid to late '80's and therefore had been an
adult, perhaps a young adult during the years of the Holocaust.  Mr. Roadburg
is dead and he could not have sworn an affidavit in these proceedings or
testified if it had not been a summary trial but he was asked on discovery what
the impact [on] him had been of this particular passage in the letter.

[48]      At question 915, he says:

To -- I am not going
to try to think what he had in mind or whatever, but it, there it is, and
that's the end of it as far as I'm concerned.  To have that, -- harbour that
feeling and to even compare -- compare his relationship or service or his work
for me to that scene is obscene, absolutely obscene.

[49]      At 964:

I didn't know what
he was talking about.  All I know is that he used the comparison that I treated
him, knowingly or unknow­ingly I treated him so badly.  That he’d even think
that anyone could be so heartless and cruel.  I just could not accept it.

[50]      At 967:

I decided I could
never work with him.  I could never work with him.

[51]      At 1036:

The statement, this
is a man that’s harbours these feelings and I don't want -- I can't be near
him.

[52]      Mr. Wise, on his discovery said at
question 1863 and this is the question:

Did you not take
into consideration that the use of that phraseology with him might be very
offensive?

[53]      Answer:

I couldn't have
cared less.  He hasn't cared less about me, period.

[54]
Given that Mr. Wise held on to
that letter of June 23rd, 1999 for some 18 months out of the concern over the
effect it would have on Mr. Roadburg's health and the fact known to Mr. Wise,
Mr. Roadburg was Jewish, it is hard to imagine that Mr. Wise could have come up
with a more offensive comment.

[55]      I cannot
say that Mr. Roadburg's reaction to the offensive portion of the June 21st 1999
letter was disproportionate.
I accept that so far as Mr. Roadburg was
concerned, the ill-advised comparison drawn by Mr. Wise between his treatment
by Mr. Roadburg and the treatment of the Jews as forced labourers irretrievably
destroyed any chance of a workable relationship between Mr. Roadburg and Mr.
Wise.

[Emphasis added.]

[
18
]

The trial judge returned to the threat to sue
and gave it a cumulative effect in his conclusion:

[57]      The
threatened lawsuit may not have been enough in and of itself to constitute
cause for summary dismissal but I find the combination in this case of the
threat to sue and the unfortunate reference to the Jews and their use as forced
labour, in the circumstances known to both parties at the time, and in the
particular circumstances of these individuals, does constitute cause for summary
dismissal and the plaintiff's claim for damages for wrongful dismissal is
dismissed.

[
19
]

On appeal Wise argues that the trial judge made
too much of his hyperbole and did not fairly put his words in the context of a
favourable employment history of almost 10 years.

[
20
]

In my view the decision can be upheld solely on
the finding in connection with the insult, without reference to the threat, if
that is what it was.  I prefer not to express an opinion on that aspect of the
case.  The trial judge's conclusion about the effect of the insult on the
employment relationship is bound up in his appreciation of the evidence and it
is not palpably wrong.  That being so, we cannot interfere with the result.

[
21
]

I would dismiss the appeal.

“The Honourable Mr. Justice Donald”

I agree:

“The
Honourable Madam Justice Prowse”

I agree:

“The Honourable Madam Justice Kirkpatrick”
